js_003: Which Korean writer wrote The Square?
js_008: The Square is a novel Choe In-hun published in 1960. It’s a landmark of postwar literature that took on division and ideology head-on.
js_010: What’s the name of the philosophy student at the heart of The Square?
js_015: The protagonist is Lee Myeong-jun — a philosophy student who crosses between South and North in search of an ideal place to live.
js_017: Which two spaces does the novel set against each other?
js_018: The private room and the square
js_021: The ideal and the real world
js_022: The novel’s backbone is the contrast between the private room and the square — a person’s private space versus the shared public space.
js_024: What does ‘the private room’ most nearly symbolize in the novel?
js_025: A person’s own private, personal space
js_026: The state’s prisons and interrogation rooms
js_027: A wide public square where people come and go
js_028: Trenches and bunkers on a battlefield
js_029: The private room is a personal, private domain no one else can invade. Myeong-jun sees the South as a place of nothing but private rooms.
js_031: What does ‘the square’ most nearly symbolize in the novel?
js_032: The public sphere where people live together
js_033: A hidden little room to hide away alone
js_034: A crowded market street packed with people
js_035: The underworld where the dead dwell
js_036: The square is the public space where people live and mingle together — the ideal Myeong-jun keeps searching for to the end.
js_038: As a POW, Myeong-jun chooses neither South nor North — but what?
js_043: Myeong-jun picks neither South nor North but a neutral country — because he found no true square in either system.
js_045: What’s the name of the Indian merchant ship Myeong-jun boards for the neutral country?
js_050: Myeong-jun’s ship is the Indian merchant vessel the Tagore. The final scene unfolds on the night it crosses the South China Sea.
js_052: How does Myeong-jun’s story end during the voyage?
js_053: He throws himself into the blue sea
js_056: He falls ill aboard and dies
js_057: During the voyage Myeong-jun plunges into the blue sea. That sea becomes the last square he had been seeking.
js_059: Which 1960 event let the author confront the issue of division head-on?
js_064: The author said the April Revolution is what let him write about division openly — the moment the taboo on expression collapsed.
js_066: When did The Square first appear in the world?
js_067: In 1960, just after the April Revolution
js_069: 1951, in the thick of the Korean War
js_071: The Square appeared in 1960 in the magazine Saebyeok (‘Dawn’). It came out as a book the following year.
js_081: Choe In-hun (1934–2018) was born in Hoeryong and moved South during the Korean War. In works like The Gray Man and A Dream of Nine Clouds he probed ideas and existence.
js_082: Lee Myeong-jun is a philosophy student. His cerebral yet deeply yearning nature drives the whole novel.
js_083: The private room and the square are the novel’s two keywords — the conviction that private freedom (the private room) and public life (the square) must exist together.
js_084: Myeong-jun sees the South as all private rooms with an empty square — a disillusionment that everyone chases self-interest and no public ideal remains.
js_085: The square is the public space where people live together — the ideal Myeong-jun searches for as he crosses between South and North.
js_086: As a POW, Myeong-jun chooses a neutral country over South or North — because neither system offered a harmony of private room and square.
js_087: The Tagore is the Indian merchant ship carrying POWs to a neutral country. Tellingly, it’s named after the Indian poet Tagore.
js_088: During the voyage Myeong-jun throws himself into the blue sea. In a sense he completes at sea the square that never existed on land.
js_089: The April Revolution (1960) was a citizens’ uprising that toppled the Syngman Rhee dictatorship. In that air of freedom, writing openly about division became possible.
js_090: The Square appeared in the magazine Saebyeok in 1960 and became a book the next year. The spirit of the moment right after April 19 runs deep through it.
js_104: A personal, private space no one else can invade. Myeong-jun sees the South as overflowing with private rooms and an empty square — a society where everyone hides in their own room.
js_105: The public space where people live together — the ideal Myeong-jun keeps chasing across South and North. It’s the keyword paired with the private room.
js_106: A philosophy student who longs for a true life. Chasing his ideal, he is disillusioned again and again in both South and North — the novel’s cerebral protagonist.
js_108: Yun-ae, his lover in the South; Eun-hye, his lover and a dancer in the North. Eun-hye dies on the battlefield carrying his child, driving Myeong-jun to his final despair.
js_110: The South’s indolence and license, the North’s hollow slogans. The novel takes neither side, criticizing both systems at once.
js_112: POW Myeong-jun chooses a neutral country over South or North and boards the Indian ship the Tagore — his conclusion that no true square exists anywhere.
js_113: The sea Myeong-jun throws himself into. It reads as a symbol of the true square that never existed on land. The vision of two gulls draws him there.
js_115: The writer who confronted division openly in the freedom of April 19. He revised The Square many times, refining even the gulls’ meaning from edition to edition.
js_118: Choe In-hun’s signature novel, published in the magazine Saebyeok in 1960.
js_119: The freedom opened by the April Revolution made it possible to write about division head-on.
js_120: It weighs South and North together through two keywords: the private room and the square.
js_121: It’s philosophy student Lee Myeong-jun’s journey to find a place of true life.
js_123: Myeong-jun feels the South is all private rooms with an empty square.
js_124: Because his father defected North, he’s suspected of disloyalty and put through interrogation and torture.
js_125: He loves Yun-ae, but even that love can’t undo his disillusion.
js_126: In the end he despairs of the South and resolves to head North.
js_129: He crosses to the North, where his father is, hoping for a new square.
js_130: But the North’s square was filled with nothing but empty slogans.
js_131: He meets the dancer Eun-hye and finds comfort in a bleak life.
js_132: Myeong-jun realizes neither South nor North is a place of true life.
js_135: The Korean War breaks out and Myeong-jun goes to the front.
js_136: Eun-hye, serving at the front, dies carrying Myeong-jun’s child.
js_137: Myeong-jun is taken prisoner and confined to a camp.
js_138: Love and ideals collapse all at once.
js_140: The neutral country and the blue sea
js_141: At the POW repatriation he’s forced to pick South or North.
js_142: He refuses both, chooses a neutral country, and boards the Tagore.
js_143: In two gulls trailing the ship he sees his dead Eun-hye and their daughter.
js_144: One night, Myeong-jun throws himself into the blue sea.
js_146: The private room, the square, and today
js_147: It leaves us the question that a life of only the private room, or only the square, is incomplete.
js_148: It became a milestone of postwar literature that reflected on division through ideology.
js_149: Choe In-hun reworked this novel again and again across many editions.
js_150: The blue sea remains a symbol of the true square that never existed on land.
js_152: Because his father defected North, Myeong-jun is suspected of disloyalty and subjected to interrogation and violence by the Southern police — the moment when the state invades even a person’s private room.
js_153: It exposes how fragile the seemingly free private room of the South really is, and pushes Myeong-jun toward defecting North.
js_155: The dancer Eun-hye, serving at the front, dies on the battlefield carrying Myeong-jun’s child — the scene where the last love and warmth he could hold onto slips away.
js_156: When war takes not an ideology but even one person’s love, it makes us ask what choices are left to Myeong-jun.
js_158: At the POW repatriation, Myeong-jun chooses a neutral country over South or North — the decisive scene where he offers a third answer against the coercion of both systems.
js_159: Where picking one side seems obvious, it makes us think about what it means to refuse both.
js_160: A life of only the private room, or only the square — which frightens you more?
js_161: Imagine what you’d lose if only one remained — private freedom (the private room) or public solidarity (the square).
js_162: When no system offers a true life, what should a person choose?
js_163: Recall Myeong-jun’s choice of a neutral country. Refusing, too, can be a choice.
js_164: Was Myeong-jun’s plunge into the sea a defeat, or a last freedom?
js_165: If you read the blue sea as a symbol of the true square, his end can look different.
